# Change-control checklist — platform facilities

Applies to every change raised against the facility estate, including work carried out by vendors under
a framework agreement. The checklist is filled in by the change raiser and countersigned by the shift
supervisor before the ticket leaves draft.

## Before the change

- [ ] A change record exists with a single named owner, a start and end window, and a rollback step written
      by someone other than the person who will execute it.
- [ ] The rollback step names the exact state to restore and the person who verifies it afterwards.
- [ ] Any safety interlock that must be bypassed is listed, together with the mitigation that replaces it
      while the bypass is active.
- [ ] The affected room and rack are named. "Facilities" is not an acceptable location.
- [ ] A second engineer has read the plan and signed it. For changes that touch power distribution the
      reviewer must be from the electrical team.

## During the change

## Structure of a note

The first paragraph says what customers can observe, in their terms. The second says what is being done and
by whom. The third, when known, says when the next update will follow. Anything else — hypotheses, internal
tooling names, the names of engineers — is left out of the customer-facing note and recorded in the internal
timeline instead.

Internal notes carry more detail. They name the working theory, the person testing it, and the two or three
diagnostics already excluded. An internal note that lists every alarm without saying which ones were ruled
out costs the next responder the same investigation twice.

## Postmortem

A postmortem is written for every S1 and for any S2 that repeated within the quarter. It is blameless in the
narrow sense that it names systems and decisions rather than individuals, and it ends with no more than
three actions, each with an owner and a date. Postmortems with ten actions are treated as having none: the
review samples whether the actions were completed, and a list nobody finishes scores worse than a short one
that closes.

## Escalation touchpoints

Handovers are written, not spoken. A spoken handover reaches the next shift and nobody else; a written one
reaches the engineer who is called at three in the morning two weeks later and needs to know why a circuit
was left isolated.

## Standing notes

The plant rooms are visited on a walking round twice per shift. Round times are recorded, because a round
that is consistently recorded at the same minute is a round that is being signed off from the office. The
security lead samples the timestamps monthly and has, on two occasions, asked for the round to be repeated
under observation.

Rooms under construction are excluded from the round only while the contractor's permit is open, and the
exclusion ends automatically when the permit expires. An exclusion that outlives its permit is treated as a
finding in the next audit.

## Out of hours

# Export reading guide — riser assembly extracts

## Why this guide exists

The assembly exports are written by a field extractor that puts one record per line and omits the header
row. The omission is deliberate: the extractor is shared by four teams, and a header written by one team
would be wrong for the others. The order for each family is therefore recorded here and nowhere else, and
every extract names its family on its first line.

## Field order by family

| Extract family | Field order |
|---|---|
| third-riser assembly | asset identifier, certified value, test pressure, verification date |
| north-riser assembly | asset identifier, test pressure, certified value, verification date |
| low-voltage distribution | asset identifier, certified value, verification date |
| roof plant | asset identifier, test pressure, verification date |

The two riser families share a shape but not an order. A record copied from one family into a ticket for
the other parses cleanly and reads wrongly, which is why the family name is printed on the first line of
every extract and why this table is the only place the order is written down.

## Field notes

# Facility audit — changelog

Changes to the facility walkthrough audit, newest first. Each entry records what changed and the release
of the audit pack that first carried it.

## 2026-02-17 — pack 2026.02

The walkthrough audit is now run every six weeks. The previous semi-annual cadence was set when the
estate held two halls; with seven halls in scope a semi-annual pass meant that a hall could go five months
between physical inspections, which the review group judged too long to be useful.

Nothing else in the audit changed. The checklist, the evidence requirements and the sign-off chain are
identical to pack 2025.09.

## 2025-09-04 — pack 2025.09

The audit pack gained a photographic evidence requirement for cable management. Written descriptions of
cable routing had proven impossible to check against the previous pack, because two engineers describing the
same tray produced descriptions that could not be compared.

The pack also dropped the separate thermostat verification sheet. Its three checks were folded into the
environmental section, where they were already being recorded twice.

## 2025-03-11 — pack 2025.03

Both checks are automated. Their results are attached to the runbook entry, so a future reader can see that
verification happened rather than reading an assertion that it did.

## Scope note

This runbook covers service credentials only. Certificates follow the lifecycle described by the issuing
authority, and the estate does not run its own certificate authority. Licence keys are handled by
procurement and are out of scope here.

## Escalation touchpoints

The communications owner and the incident commander are different people for S1 incidents, so that one can
concentrate on the fault while the other handles the outside world. Handover between them is verbal and
recorded in the timeline, never implied. If the incident outlives two shift changes, the communications owner
writes a shift summary that a newcomer can read in under a minute without asking a question.

# Retention and evidence policy

## Purpose

This policy fixes how long operational records are kept and what counts as evidence when a decision is
challenged later. It exists because the estate has twice been asked to justify a change that nobody could
reconstruct from memory.

## What is retained

Change tickets, incident timelines and their attachments are retained for seven years. Badge logs are
retained for two years, with the exception of entries linked to an incident, which inherit the incident's
retention period. Audit packs — the signed checklist, the photographs and the reviewer's note — are retained
for seven years and are stored with the ticket rather than in a shared folder.

Recorded values published in registers are retained for the life of the asset plus three years, because a
decommissioned asset can still be the subject of a warranty claim long after the physical unit is gone.

## What is not retained

# Third-riser assembly export

Extract of the valve records for the third riser, one record per line. The extractor that produced
this file omits the header row; the order of the fields is defined in the export reading guide, and a
line that does not carry four fields is a malformed extract rather than a valve with missing data.

Records are ordered by identifier. Dates are the day the reading was verified, not the day the
valve was installed.

## During the change

The executing engineer narrates each step into the ticket as it completes, rather than reconstructing the
sequence afterwards. Where a step deviates from the plan, the deviation is recorded before the next step
begins, together with the reason and the name of whoever approved it. A change that stalls for more than
thirty minutes is either resumed with an updated plan or rolled back; it is never left half-applied while
the engineer attends to something else.

Communication runs on the change channel. Anyone who needs to know what is happening reads that channel;
nobody is expected to chase updates by message. If the change affects customer-visible service, the
communications owner posts a holding note before the first step rather than after the first symptom.

## After the change

The completion note records the finish time, the state of every interlock, and any follow-up work with an
owner and a date. Evidence — screenshots, command output, photographs of the physical state — is attached
to the ticket, not kept in a personal folder. Tickets without evidence are reopened at the weekly review.

# North-riser assembly export

Extract of the valve records for the north riser, one record per line, produced by the same extractor as
the other riser exports and therefore also without a header row. The field order for this family of
exports is defined in the export reading guide and is not the same for every riser.

Records are ordered by identifier. A line that does not carry four fields is a malformed extract.

## Method note

The ratio is computed from fifteen-minute samples, not hourly averages, because hourly averages hide exactly
the overlap the review is looking for. Samples with a known instrumentation fault are excluded and the
exclusion is listed in the appendix so that a future reader can reproduce the figure. Where a hall has less
than a full quarter of clean samples it is reported as provisional and carries no flag either way.

## Forecast

The forecast assumes the batch window does not widen. If the reconciliation jobs move into the working day,
the peak shifts rather than grows and the flags above become more urgent than their numbers suggest. The
forecast is revised after the mid-quarter checkpoint, and the revision is published as a new version of
this memo rather than as an appended paragraph, so a reader always knows which version they are holding.

## Actions

- Rebalance the batch schedule so that backup and reconciliation do not overlap. Owner: data platform.
- Order one spare unit for the hall flagged on headroom. Owner: procurement, with facilities confirming the
  physical space before the order is placed.
- Re-run the ratio calculation after the rebalance and publish the result with the next review.

None of the actions changes a tenancy. The review opens a discussion; it does not move a service, and it
does not authorise work on a hall. Those decisions belong to the change process and are recorded there.

## Method note

Where evidence is contradictory, the reviewer records both versions and the resolution, and does not delete
the version that turned out to be wrong. The record of a mistake is worth more than a clean file.

## Review

The policy is reviewed annually by the records owner and the security lead together. The review looks at
two numbers: the share of sampled tickets that carry complete evidence, and the number of deletion
exceptions granted. Both are reported to the operations group without commentary, so that the trend is read
from the numbers rather than from the framing.

Readings are taken with the loop at steady state, which the team defines as three consecutive samples inside

the same reason: the isolation valves on the eastern side do not fully seat, so a service on one loop bleeds
pressure from the other. The valves are on the maintenance backlog with a date and an owner, and until they
are replaced the two loops are scheduled apart.

# Calibration record — east-aisle cooling loop

## Asset

The east-aisle cooling loop is asset NBL-118 in the facility registry. It serves the two aisle rows on the
eastern side of the north hall and shares a return manifold with the southern loop; the shared manifold is
the reason the two loops are never serviced on the same day.

## Re-measurement

The loop was re-measured during the February window after the quarterly review flagged a drift between the
commissioning figure and the figure recorded on the local gauge. Both readings were taken at the same supply
temperature, fifteen minutes apart, with the secondary pump running and the bypass closed.

explicitly: a re-measurement that confirms the existing value is still a re-measurement and is recorded as

# Capacity review — Q1 memo

The quarterly capacity review compares peak demand against provisioned headroom for each hall, and flags any
hall whose peak-to-average ratio exceeds four. Recorded values for the quarter are held in the calibration
register rather than in this memo, so that a single figure has a single home.

## Summary for the quarter

Demand grew in two halls and was flat in the rest. The growth is concentrated in the batch window between
02:00 and 05:00, when reconciliation jobs overlap with the nightly backup. Outside that window the halls run
at their usual profile, which is why an average-based view understates the pressure.

Three halls were flagged. Two were flagged on the ratio and one on absolute headroom: it can clear the ratio
test and still be one failed unit away from a hard limit, and the review treats both conditions as flags
with the same review path.

# Access control — facility policy, section 3

## 3.1 Badge tiers

The estate recognises four badge tiers. A tier-1 badge opens the shared entrances and the meeting rooms on
the first floor. A tier-2 badge adds the operations floor and the shared workshop. A tier-3 badge adds the
plant rooms on a named list, and a tier-4 badge adds everything on that list plus the network core.

Tier changes are requested by the line manager and approved by the site security lead. Requests are
processed in the weekly access review, not on demand, unless the requester's manager is willing to page the
security lead outside hours and record the reason for the exception.

## 3.2 Escorted access

Contractors hold no standing tier. They are issued a visitor badge that expires at the end of the working
day and they are escorted at all times inside the plant rooms. The escort is a named member of staff, not a
group; an escort who is called away hands the visitor back to reception rather than leaving them seated in
a corridor.

# Escalation matrix and shift handover

## Matrix

| Trigger | First contact | Second contact | Third contact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alarm in a plant room | platform on-call engineer | duty manager | director of engineering |
| Customer-visible loss | platform on-call engineer | incident commander | director of engineering |
| Access control fault | site security lead | platform on-call engineer | duty manager |
| Vendor on site without a ticket | shift supervisor | site security lead | vendor account owner |

The first contact is made by whoever observes the trigger. Nobody waits for permission to escalate; the
matrix exists to remove the question of whom to call, not to limit who may call.

## Handover

Each shift ends with a handover that covers three things: what is in flight, what is waiting on someone
else, and what looks wrong but has no ticket yet. The third item is the most valuable and the most often
omitted, so the handover template lists it first.

## Method note

the overlap the review is looking for. Samples with a known instrumentation fault are excluded and the
exclusion is listed in the appendix so that a future reader can reproduce the figure. Where a hall has less
than a full quarter of clean samples it is reported as provisional and carries no flag either way.

reaches the engineer who is called at three in the morning two weeks later and needs to know why a circuit
was left isolated.

## Standing notes

that is consistently recorded at the same minute is a round that is being signed off from the office. The
security lead samples the timestamps monthly and has, on two occasions, asked for the round to be repeated
under observation.

exclusion ends automatically when the permit expires. An exclusion that outlives its permit is treated as a
finding in the next audit.

## Forecast

The forecast assumes the batch window does not widen. If the reconciliation jobs move into the working day,
the peak shifts rather than grows and the flags above become more urgent than their numbers suggest. The
forecast is revised after the mid-quarter checkpoint, and the revision is published as a new version of
this memo rather than as an appended paragraph, so a reader always knows which version they are holding.

## Actions

- Rebalance the batch schedule so that backup and reconciliation do not overlap. Owner: data platform.
- Order one spare unit for the hall flagged on headroom. Owner: procurement, with facilities confirming the
  physical space before the order is placed.
- Re-run the ratio calculation after the rebalance and publish the result with the next review.

None of the actions changes a tenancy. The review opens a discussion; it does not move a service, and it
does not authorise work on a hall. Those decisions belong to the change process and are recorded there.

# Export reading guide — riser assembly extracts

## Why this guide exists

The assembly exports are written by a field extractor that puts one record per line and omits the header
row. The omission is deliberate: the extractor is shared by four teams, and a header written by one team
would be wrong for the others. The order for each family is therefore recorded here and nowhere else, and
every extract names its family on its first line.

## Field order by family

| Extract family | Field order |
|---|---|
| third-riser assembly | asset identifier, certified value, test pressure, verification date |
| north-riser assembly | asset identifier, test pressure, certified value, verification date |
| low-voltage distribution | asset identifier, certified value, verification date |
| roof plant | asset identifier, test pressure, verification date |

The two riser families share a shape but not an order. A record copied from one family into a ticket for
the other parses cleanly and reads wrongly, which is why the family name is printed on the first line of
every extract and why this table is the only place the order is written down.

## Method

# Access control — facility policy, section 3

## 3.1 Badge tiers

The estate recognises four badge tiers. A tier-1 badge opens the shared entrances and the meeting rooms on
the first floor. A tier-2 badge adds the operations floor and the shared workshop. A tier-3 badge adds the
plant rooms on a named list, and a tier-4 badge adds everything on that list plus the network core.

Tier changes are requested by the line manager and approved by the site security lead. Requests are
processed in the weekly access review, not on demand, unless the requester's manager is willing to page the
security lead outside hours and record the reason for the exception.

## 3.2 Escorted access

Contractors hold no standing tier. They are issued a visitor badge that expires at the end of the working
day and they are escorted at all times inside the plant rooms. The escort is a named member of staff, not a
group; an escort who is called away hands the visitor back to reception rather than leaving them seated in
a corridor.

## Method note

The ratio is computed from fifteen-minute samples, not hourly averages, because hourly averages hide exactly
the overlap the review is looking for. Samples with a known instrumentation fault are excluded and the
exclusion is listed in the appendix so that a future reader can reproduce the figure. Where a hall has less
than a full quarter of clean samples it is reported as provisional and carries no flag either way.

# Escalation matrix and shift handover

## Matrix

| Trigger | First contact | Second contact | Third contact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alarm in a plant room | platform on-call engineer | duty manager | director of engineering |
| Customer-visible loss | platform on-call engineer | incident commander | director of engineering |
| Access control fault | site security lead | platform on-call engineer | duty manager |
| Vendor on site without a ticket | shift supervisor | site security lead | vendor account owner |

The first contact is made by whoever observes the trigger. Nobody waits for permission to escalate; the
matrix exists to remove the question of whom to call, not to limit who may call.

## Handover

Each shift ends with a handover that covers three things: what is in flight, what is waiting on someone
else, and what looks wrong but has no ticket yet. The third item is the most valuable and the most often
omitted, so the handover template lists it first.

## Method

Readings are taken with the loop at steady state, which the team defines as three consecutive samples inside
a two-percent band. Sampling before steady state is the most common source of spurious drift reports, and it
is the first thing the calibration team checks when an operator reports a value that "moved overnight".

Two engineers take the reading independently when the value is being revised. Where their readings differ by
more than the tolerance, both are recorded and the asset is scheduled for a third reading rather than
averaging the two, because an average of two disagreeing measurements hides whichever one is wrong.

## Follow-up

The shared manifold remains on the watch list. It has been flagged twice in three quarters, both times for
the same reason: the isolation valves on the eastern side do not fully seat, so a service on one loop bleeds
pressure from the other. The valves are on the maintenance backlog with a date and an owner, and until they
are replaced the two loops are scheduled apart.
